title: First jazz concert in Philadelphia, 1936, and the Journeys concerts
summary: Rose describes producing the first listening concert of authentic jazz in 1936 at age twenty, being mistaken for a kid at Symphony Hall, and the roughly 196 Journeys concerts ending in 1967.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: My first actual public activity in jazz was when I ran a jazz concert for the American Newspaper Guild in Philadelphia at Mercantile Hall. And that was in 1936, in January of 1936. And it included Sidney Bechet and Sidney D. Paris, members of Jack Teagarden's band who were playing upstairs for dancing. That included Sterling Boze and Boze and Irving Fazola. And a local clarinet player by the name of Billy Kretschmer was there. As far as I know, this is the first actual concert ever held of authentic jazz in which people came to buy tickets and sit down to listen. Well, you couldn't have been too old then. I was twenty. Did that cause you any problems? Yeah, it did, because I looked a lot younger than I was. And, uh, but having left home as early as I did, I was already experienced in, in, uh, compensating for all those problems.
Oh. What about, did you, did you have any trouble, uh, getting in? Have I, didn't you tell me something about that once? Are you, people didn't recognize you as the producer?

Oh, yeah. I, um, uh, I particularly had written that thing about the time I was in Symphony Hall in Boston running a concert there. And, uh, I had gone out for a cup of coffee or sandwich or something. And on my way back in, uh, the guard wouldn't let me in because he assumed that I was a kid trying to crash it. And when I explained to him who I was, he didn't believe me. And at last I had to get them to call backstage and Muggsy Spank came out and identified me and we went in. How many journeys into jazz concerts were there? Uh, there were just short of two hundred. I think it was a hundred and ninety-six or a hundred and ninety-seven. The last of which was in Carbondale, Illinois in nineteen sixty-seven. Do you plan to do any more concert? No, I really, uh, I don't think I'll ever do another concert because I don't think I can ever reassemble the quality of music that I consider to be essential for the proper presentation of jazz.
